title: The construct state

objectives.can: Recognise a noun in the construct state and read a construct chain as 'X of Y'.
Recognise ten more common nouns, with their construct forms.

explanation.summary: Greek and Latin put the possessor in the genitive. Hebrew does something different: it keeps the possessor as it is and alters the thing possessed, which stands in a short 'construct' form and leans on the next word. This is how Hebrew says 'the word of the Lord' and 'the sons of Israel'.

sections.heading: Two states of a noun
body: Every Hebrew noun has an absolute state and a construct state. The absolute is the form you meet in a dictionary or when a noun stands alone. The construct is the form it takes when it is joined to the noun that follows it, and it is usually shorter. The corpus records this as State: Abs or Cons.

Two nouns joined this way form a construct chain, and it is read 'X of Y': the first noun is in the construct state, and the second, which is the last member of the chain, is in the absolute state. The English word 'of' has no Hebrew word to match it. The relation, which can be possession, source, material, kind, or something else, is read from the sense.

sections.heading: How the construct form looks
body: Many nouns change a little. The commonest changes are in the endings, and they are regular: a masculine plural ending -ִים becomes -ֵי, a feminine singular ending -ָה becomes -ַת, a dual ending -ַיִם becomes -ֵי, and a feminine plural ending -וֹת stays as it is. In the singular of many masculine nouns, vowels of the first syllables shorten, as in דָּבָר and דְּבַר. Some nouns do not change at all: מֶלֶךְ, קוֹל and לֵב look the same in both states, and there only the context tells you.

sections.heading: Reading a chain
body: Read a chain from the first word to the last, and put 'of' between them: אֶרֶץ מוֹאָב, 'the land of Moab'; בֵּית לֶחֶם, the place-name Bethlehem, whose two parts are 'house' and 'bread'. The first noun is in the construct state, and it is the one that carries the main sense: in 'the word of the Lord' it is the 'word' that is spoken of.

A chain may have more than two members. Each member except the last is in the construct state, and each one depends on the next. A chain may also contain a prefixed particle on its first word, as in בִּימֵי, 'in the days of'.

sections.heading: Definiteness belongs to the whole chain
body: The article normally stands on the last member only, and it makes the whole chain definite. פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם is 'the face of the waters', 'the face' being definite because the waters are. A construct noun almost never has an article of its own. A chain whose last member has no article is indefinite, unless that member is a name or carries a suffix, which also make the chain definite. This is why a construct chain is often 'the X of Y' in English even when you see no article.
Because the members of a chain are bound together, an adjective that describes the first noun usually comes after the whole chain, not between the two nouns.

misunderstandings: The construct is not a case ending that means 'of'. Hebrew has no word for 'of' here: the reader supplies it from the way the two nouns are joined.
A noun that looks exactly like its absolute form can still be in the construct state, and the analysed texts tell you which. Look at what follows.
The article is on the last member, not on the first. The first noun is almost never written with an article, even when the chain is translated with 'the'.
'X of Y' is only a pointer to the sense. Chains can mean 'the tree of life', 'the sons of Israel', 'the days of the judges', 'a man of war': possession, relation, quality, time or kind.

deeper.heading: A construct before a clause
body: A construct noun can be followed not by a noun but by a verb form or a whole short clause, most often in expressions of time. In Ruth 1:1, 'in the days of …' is followed by the infinitive of a verb and then the participle that is its subject. The English edition shows how such a phrase is turned into a time clause. Grammarians treat the construct there as a bound form that links a noun to what follows, not necessarily another noun.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three chains in one verse. פְּנֵי תְהוֹם is 'the face of the deep': פְּנֵי is plural construct. רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים is 'the spirit of God': רוּחַ is in construct, and אֱלֹהִים is the last member. פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם is 'the face of the waters': the article on the last word makes the whole chain definite.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God said: 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness; and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בִדְגַת הַיָּם is 'among the fish of the sea', with the prefix ב; דְגַת is the feminine singular construct, with the ending -ַת. וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם is 'and among the birds of the sky'; עוֹף is the construct and הַשָּׁמַיִם is the last member, with the article.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And out of the ground made the LORD God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: עֵץ הַחַיִּים and עֵץ הַדַּעַת are two chains: 'the tree of life' and 'the tree of the knowledge'. עֵץ is the construct in both. It looks the same as the absolute עֵץ earlier in the verse (in 'every tree that is pleasant', the words כָּל and עֵץ), so here only the next word shows the state.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And the name of the man was Elimelech, and the name of his wife Naomi, and the name of his two sons Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites of Beth-lehem in Judah. And they came into the field of Moab, and continued there.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וְשֵׁם הָאִישׁ is 'and the name of the man': a construct and a last member with the article. שְׁנֵי בָנָיו is 'two of his sons': the dual construct of the word for 'two' before a noun with a suffix. שְׂדֵי מוֹאָב is 'the fields of Moab': a plural construct and a name.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: AND IT came to pass in the days when the judges judged, that there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Beth-lehem in Judah went to sojourn in the field of Moab, he, and his wife, and his two sons.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בִּימֵי is 'in the days of', with the prefix ב and the plural construct of the word for 'day'. What follows is an infinitive in the construct form and then a participle with the article, so the whole phrase says 'in the days when the judges judged'. בִּשְׂדֵי מוֹאָב is 'in the fields of Moab'.
